error_modes.label: Altitude control during the instrument procedure

texts.0: SP, due to an unstabilized power and pitch relationship during the instrument segment, failed to hold the assigned altitude within the published tolerance. Deviations reached 400 to 500 feet and the trend continued unchecked through the level-off. IP intervened on the controls to re-establish the assigned altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to late recognition of the vertical velocity trend approaching level-off, allowed altitude to reach the 300 feet limit. The correction was started only after verbal prompting from the IP and was slow to arrest the trend. Altitude was regained, but the SP remained at the limit for the remainder of the segment.
texts.2: SP, due to a coarse power reduction at level-off, allowed altitude to drift about 220 feet below the assigned value. SP detected the deviation on the altimeter and vertical velocity indicator and corrected back inside 150 feet without IP input. The rest of the segment was held within tolerance.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude within 150 feet throughout the instrument procedure. Level-offs were anticipated with a timely lead point and a matching power change. The few small excursions were detected by cross-check and corrected promptly.
texts.4: SP held the assigned altitude with excursions of no more than a few tens of feet, including through configuration and heading changes. Level-offs were anticipated and trimmed off, so no correction was needed after capture. Vertical control stayed precise for the whole procedure.
texts.marginal: SP kept altitude within standards, but the deviations clustered in the outer half of the band, particularly after configuration changes. The corrections were correct in direction yet repeatedly reactive rather than anticipatory. SP is expected to tighten vertical control by leading each level-off with power and trim.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the power and pitch changes and the trend on the vertical velocity indicator, SP followed on the controls through the segment while beginning to include the altimeter in the scan. Anticipating level-off with a lead point and a matching power change, without a reminder, has not yet been asked of SP at this stage. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin naming the lead point for level-off before setting the power change independently.
texts_at.1: SP held the assigned altitude inside the tolerance required at this stage, with the deviation settling at about 280 feet near each level-off. The margin traces to the vertical velocity trend being recognized a beat after level-off begins rather than while it is still developing. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to recognize the vertical velocity trend earlier so the margin at level-off narrows.
texts_at.2: SP kept the assigned altitude inside the tolerance required at this stage, with the excursion settling at about 220 feet after a coarse power reduction at level-off. The deviation traces to the power change being sized by feel rather than to a known setting for the transition. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to use a known power setting at level-off so the excursion narrows further.
texts_at.3: SP held the assigned altitude within about 120 feet through the procedure, the small excursion tracing to the lead point for level-off being taken a moment later than ideal. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to take the lead point for level-off a little earlier so this small excursion is removed.

texts_above.1: SP held the assigned altitude to about 270 feet near each level-off, the correction following a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP detected the deviation on the altimeter and vertical velocity indicator and corrected back inside about 220 feet without IP input, after a power reduction at level-off sized by feel. Using a known power setting at level-off, rather than sizing it by feel, would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude control during the procedure.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude within about 120 feet throughout the instrument procedure, level-offs anticipated with a timely lead point and a matching power change so the few small excursions were detected by cross-check and corrected promptly. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to very good altitude control during the procedure.
texts_above.4: SP held the assigned altitude with excursions of no more than a few tens of feet, including through configuration and heading changes, level-offs anticipated and trimmed off so no correction was needed after capture. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to excellent altitude control during the procedure.

error_modes.label: Airspeed control during the instrument procedure

texts.0: SP, due to power settings applied without reference to the resulting airspeed, failed to hold the procedural airspeed. Deviations exceeded 20 KIAS on the descent and again in the level segment, with speed decaying further as configuration changed. IP directed and then set the required power to recover the profile.
texts.1: SP, due to delayed power correction after the descent was established, allowed airspeed to reach the 20 KIAS limit. The correction was applied only after the IP called the deviation and then overshot in the opposite direction. Airspeed control stayed at the tolerance limit for the rest of the segment.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow power adjustment when configuration was changed, allowed airspeed to vary by about 15 KIAS. SP identified the trend on the airspeed indicator and restored the procedural speed inside 10 KIAS without prompting. No further excursion followed.
texts.3: SP maintained the procedural airspeed within 10 KIAS through level flight, descent and configuration changes. Power was adjusted in anticipation of each change rather than in reaction to it. Small excursions were trapped early by cross-check.
texts.4: SP held the procedural airspeed with variations of only a few knots for the entire procedure. Power and configuration changes were coordinated so that speed remained essentially constant. Speed control was accurate and required no follow-up correction.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within airspeed standards, but the excursions ran consistently to the fast side after descent entry. Corrections were adequate yet late enough to need a second adjustment each time. SP is expected to set and hold known power settings so that speed stays close to the target value.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the power setting for each configuration change, SP followed on the throttle while beginning to include the airspeed indicator in the cross-check. Anticipating a configuration change with power, rather than reacting to the airspeed after it moves, has not yet been asked of SP. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin naming the configuration change before it happens before setting the power change unaided.
texts_at.1: SP held the procedural airspeed inside the tolerance required at this stage, settling at about 18 KIAS from the target. The margin traces to the power correction after the descent being applied a beat later than the profile called for. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply the power correction at the same point the descent is established so the margin narrows.
texts_at.2: SP kept the procedural airspeed inside the tolerance required at this stage, varying by about 15 KIAS at a configuration change. The margin traces to the power adjustment being made a little slowly relative to the change itself. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to adjust power at the same moment as the configuration change so the margin narrows further.
texts_at.3: SP held the procedural airspeed within about 7 KIAS through level flight, descent and configuration changes, the small margin tracing to power being anticipated a moment later than ideal for one change. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to anticipate every configuration change with power so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP held the procedural airspeed to about 19 KIAS from the target, the power correction following a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified the trend on the airspeed indicator and restored the procedural speed inside about 15 KIAS without prompting, after a power adjustment made a little slowly at a configuration change. Adjusting power at the same moment as the configuration change, rather than a little after it, would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound airspeed control during the procedure.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the procedural airspeed within about 7 KIAS through level flight, descent and configuration changes, power adjusted in anticipation of each change rather than in reaction to it. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed airspeed control during the procedure.
texts_above.4: SP held the procedural airspeed with variations of only a few knots for the entire procedure, power and configuration changes coordinated so that speed remained essentially constant. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exceptional airspeed control during the procedure.

error_modes.label: Heading control during the instrument procedure

texts.0: SP, due to uncoordinated bank inputs and an abandoned heading reference, failed to hold the assigned heading. Deviations exceeded 10 degrees and the aircraft continued to diverge from the intended course without correction. IP intervened to return the aircraft to the assigned heading.
texts.1: SP, due to failure to check the roll-out heading against the assigned value, drifted out to the 10 degrees limit. The correction began only after the IP prompted verbally and was applied as a single large bank input. Heading remained at the limit until the next turn.
texts.2: SP, due to an undershot roll-out from the turn, settled about 8 degrees off the assigned heading. SP cross-checked the HSI, applied a measured correction and re-established the heading inside 5 degrees unprompted. The following turns were rolled out on heading.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned heading within 5 degrees and rolled out on the briefed headings. Turns were flown with a steady bank and adequate lead was taken for roll-out. Small excursions were corrected before they could develop.
texts.4: SP flew the assigned headings with excursions of a degree or two and rolled out on the target value on every turn. Bank was steady and coordinated, with no wandering between corrections. Directional control was consistently precise.
texts.marginal: SP held heading within standards, but drifted repeatedly to the same side between corrections instead of holding a stable reference. The corrections were correct in direction yet delivered in noticeable steps. SP is expected to keep a steady heading reference and correct in small, early increments.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the roll-out heading and the bank needed for each turn, SP followed on the controls while beginning to include the heading indicator in the scan through the turn. Judging the lead for roll-out against the turn rate actually flown has not yet been asked of SP independently. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin calling the roll-out heading during the turn before judging the lead unaided.
texts_at.1: SP held the assigned heading inside the tolerance required at this stage, settling at about 9 degrees off after roll-out from a turn. The margin traces to the roll-out heading being checked a beat after wings level rather than anticipated during the turn. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check the roll-out heading during the turn, not after it, so the margin narrows.
texts_at.2: SP kept the assigned heading inside the tolerance required at this stage, settling at about 7 degrees off after an undershot roll-out. The margin traces to the lead for roll-out being judged a little short of the turn rate actually flown. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to judge the roll-out lead against the actual turn rate so the margin narrows further.
texts_at.3: SP held the assigned heading within about 3 degrees on the turns flown, the small margin tracing to bank being eased a moment before wings level rather than held to it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to hold bank steady to wings level so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP held the assigned heading to about 9 degrees off after roll-out from a turn, the correction following a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP cross-checked the HSI, applied a measured correction and re-established the heading inside about 7 degrees unprompted, after an undershot roll-out from the turn. Judging the roll-out lead against the actual turn rate, rather than a fixed lead, would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid heading control during the procedure.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the assigned heading within about 3 degrees and rolled out on the briefed headings, turns flown with a steady bank and adequate lead taken for roll-out. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to well-developed heading control during the procedure.
texts_above.4: SP flew the assigned headings with excursions of a degree or two and rolled out on the target value on every turn, bank steady and coordinated with no wandering between corrections. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding heading control during the procedure.

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention remained fixed on a single indication, lost awareness of the aircraft state during the procedure. Pitch, bank and airspeed trends developed at the same time and none was detected by the SP. IP intervened to recover the aircraft and re-establish the required cross-check.
texts.1: SP, due to a cross-check that stalled on one display, detected the developing deviations only after they had reached the tolerance limits. Scan was restored after IP prompting but narrowed again later in the procedure. Aircraft control was recovered without intervention on the controls, but only after repeated verbal cues.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check that slowed during a workload peak, allowed two parameters to drift toward the middle of the tolerance band. SP recognized the narrowing scan, redistributed attention across the flight and navigation instruments and corrected in good time. No further lapse occurred and no IP input was needed.
texts.3: SP maintained an active cross-check across the flight and navigation instruments throughout the procedure. Deviations were detected while still small and were corrected immediately. Scan rate was sustained through configuration changes and radio work.
texts.4: SP sustained a disciplined and evenly distributed cross-check for the whole procedure, including the highest workload segments. Trends were identified before they became deviations, so the corrections needed were minimal. Attention was shared between aircraft control and navigation with no loss on either.
texts.marginal: SP kept an adequate cross-check overall, but it narrowed noticeably whenever radio or navigation tasks were added. Parameters were still contained within standards, although detection was slightly late each time. SP is expected to protect scan rate under task loading so that deviations are caught earlier.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling attention back to the panel whenever the scan stalled, SP followed the cross-check on the flight instruments and needed the reminder on two occasions during the procedure. Distributing attention across the panel without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP at this stage. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin recognizing a stalled scan without a prompt before the whole procedure is flown unaided.
texts_at.1: SP maintained the instrument cross-check inside the standard required at this stage, detecting developing deviations close to the tolerance limits. The trend traces to the scan stalling briefly on one display before continuing around the panel. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the scan moving through that display rather than stalling on it, so deviations are caught with more margin.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the instrument cross-check inside the standard required at this stage, with two parameters drifting toward the middle of the tolerance band during a workload peak. The trend traces to the scan slowing rather than stopping under that workload. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the scan rate constant through workload peaks so the drift narrows further.
texts_at.3: SP kept an active cross-check across the flight and navigation instruments, small deviations detected while still forming and corrected immediately, the trend tracing to the scan narrowing briefly during radio work rather than staying fully distributed. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to protect the scan during radio work so it stays fully distributed.

texts_above.1: SP maintained the instrument cross-check across the procedure, needing a single verbal call from the IP to restart the scan after it stalled on one display. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the narrowing scan, redistributed attention across the flight and navigation instruments and corrected in good time, after two parameters had drifted toward the middle of the tolerance band during a workload peak. Keeping the scan rate constant through the peak, rather than recognizing the narrowing afterward, would remove even that drift. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady instrument cross-check discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained an active cross-check across the flight and navigation instruments throughout the procedure, deviations detected while still small and corrected immediately, scan rate sustained through configuration changes and radio work. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate instrument cross-check discipline.
texts_above.4: SP sustained a disciplined and evenly distributed cross-check for the whole procedure, including the highest workload segments, trends identified before they became deviations so corrections needed were minimal. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exemplary instrument cross-check discipline.

error_modes.label: Navigation aid set-up, identification and course tracking

texts.0: SP, due to omitting identification of the navigation aid and selecting an incorrect course, flew the procedure on unverified guidance. The course indications were misinterpreted and the aircraft tracked away from the intended path. IP stopped the procedure and directed the correct set-up and course interception.
texts.1: SP, due to tuning the navigation receiver and selecting the course late, entered the segment without confirmed identification. The omission was corrected only after the IP prompted, and course interception was delayed as a result. Guidance was eventually valid, but the set-up stayed behind the aircraft.
texts.2: SP, due to a rushed sequence, tuned the correct frequency but confirmed identification after starting the turn toward course. SP noticed the omission, completed identification and verified course selection before the intercept. Tracking then remained on the published course without IP input.
texts.3: SP tuned, identified and verified the navigation aid and course before each segment of the procedure. Bearing and course indications were interpreted correctly and cross-checked against the published procedure. Tracking was re-established promptly after each intercept.
texts.4: SP completed navigation set-up, identification and course verification well ahead of every segment and cross-checked a backup indication each time. Interpretation of the indications was immediate and correct throughout. Course tracking was maintained with no measurable displacement.
texts.marginal: SP completed navigation set-up, identification and course selection correctly, but consistently close to the point where the guidance was needed. Nothing was missed, yet no margin was left to absorb a set-up error. SP is expected to complete tuning, identification and course selection earlier in each segment.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the frequency to tune and confirming identification before each segment, SP followed the set-up on the panel while beginning to read back the identification. Sequencing tuning, identification and course selection without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin tuning the aid on the IP's cue before completing the sequence independently.
texts_at.1: SP completed navigation set-up, identification and course selection inside the standard required at this stage, with identification confirmed close to the point guidance was needed. The trend traces to tuning being started only when the segment itself began rather than before it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to tune and identify the aid before the segment begins so identification is confirmed with more margin.
texts_at.2: SP completed navigation set-up, identification and course selection inside the standard required at this stage, with identification confirmed after the turn toward course had already started. The trend traces to the sequence being rushed rather than started earlier in the segment. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the set-up sequence earlier in the segment so identification comes before the turn.
texts_at.3: SP tuned, identified and verified the navigation aid and course before each segment, the small margin tracing to the cross-check of a backup indication being made a moment after the primary rather than with it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to cross-check the backup indication together with the primary so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP tuned, identified and verified the navigation aid and course for each segment, the identification confirmed close to the point guidance was needed after a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP noticed the omission, completed identification and verified course selection before the intercept, unaided, after starting the turn toward course before confirming identification. Starting the set-up sequence earlier in the segment, rather than rushing it at the turn, would remove even that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable navigation aid set-up technique.
texts_above.3: SP tuned, identified and verified the navigation aid and course before each segment of the procedure, bearing and course indications interpreted correctly and cross-checked against the published procedure. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good navigation aid set-up technique.
texts_above.4: SP completed navigation set-up, identification and course verification well ahead of every segment and cross-checked a backup indication each time, interpretation of the indications immediate and correct throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to superior navigation aid set-up technique.

error_modes.label: Sequence of procedural steps, checks and configuration

texts.0: SP, due to working the procedure out of sequence, failed to complete the required checks and configuration changes at the published points. The descent was started with the aircraft unconfigured and required items were left undone. IP had to sequence the procedure and direct the configuration.
texts.1: SP, due to falling behind the aircraft, reached the descent point with the approach checks still pending. The sequence was completed only after IP prompting, and the delay compressed the remainder of the procedure. All items were eventually accomplished, but not at the published points.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed start of the approach checks, was slightly behind the profile in the initial segment. SP recognized the compression, re-sequenced the remaining actions and had the aircraft configured before the descent point. The rest of the procedure was flown in the correct order and unaided.
texts.3: SP accomplished the procedural steps and configuration changes in the correct order and at the published points. Checks were completed before each transition and did not interfere with aircraft control. The SP stayed ahead of the aircraft throughout.
texts.4: SP ran the procedure with checks and configuration changes completed early at every point, leaving full capacity for aircraft control. Sequencing stayed smooth and unhurried even where the segments were short. At no stage was the SP behind the aircraft.
texts.marginal: SP kept the procedure in the correct sequence, but each step was accomplished close to its published point with little margin. Aircraft control was maintained, although workload peaked at every transition. SP is expected to move the checks and configuration changes earlier so that margin is built into each segment.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling each procedural step and configuration change at its published point, SP followed the sequence on the controls and needed the call for two of the transitions. Sequencing the checks and configuration changes without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP at this stage. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin one procedural step from memory before the whole sequence is flown unaided.
texts_at.1: SP accomplished the procedural steps and configuration changes inside the standard required at this stage, reaching the descent point with the approach checks close to complete. The trend traces to the checks being started only once the descent point was near rather than earlier in the segment. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to start the approach checks earlier in the segment so they are complete with more margin at the descent point.
texts_at.2: SP accomplished the procedural steps and configuration changes inside the standard required at this stage, slightly behind the profile in the initial segment before the sequence was re-established. The trend traces to the approach checks starting a little later than the segment allowed for. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the approach checks at the same point on every approach so the sequence does not compress.
texts_at.3: SP accomplished the procedural steps and configuration changes in the correct order and close to the published points, the small margin tracing to one check being completed a moment after its published point rather than at it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to complete that check at its published point so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP accomplished the procedural steps and configuration changes in sequence, reaching the descent point with the approach checks completed after a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the compression, re-sequenced the remaining actions and had the aircraft configured before the descent point, unaided, after starting the approach checks a little late in the initial segment. Starting the approach checks at the same point on every approach, rather than recovering the sequence afterward, would remove even that compression. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured procedural sequencing.
texts_above.3: SP accomplished the procedural steps and configuration changes in the correct order and at the published points, checks completed before each transition without interfering with aircraft control, staying ahead of the aircraft throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to precise procedural sequencing.
texts_above.4: SP ran the procedure with checks and configuration changes completed early at every point, leaving full capacity for aircraft control, sequencing smooth and unhurried even where the segments were short. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate procedural sequencing.

error_modes.label: Holding entry, pattern and drift correction

texts.0: SP, due to failure to determine the entry from the inbound course, entered holding on an incorrect pattern and did not fly the published leg orientation. Leg timing was never started and the pattern drifted well off the protected side. IP took control of the entry and re-established the correct pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to a late entry decision at the fix, flew an entry that only marginally matched the published pattern. Leg timing and drift correction were applied after the IP pointed out the displacement. The following circuit was flown correctly, but the first one was not usable.
texts.2: SP, due to under-applied drift correction outbound, arrived at the inbound turn displaced from the pattern. SP identified the error from the course indication and the leg timing, adjusted the outbound correction and stabilized the next circuit. No IP input was required.
texts.3: SP determined the correct entry, flew the published pattern and applied drift correction so that the inbound legs rolled out on course. Timing was started and adjusted at the correct points. The circuits were flown consistently.
texts.4: SP flew the entry and the holding pattern with the inbound course captured precisely and leg timing corrected to the target value from the first circuit. Drift was assessed early and applied accurately on the outbound leg. The pattern was repeatable and needed no further adjustment.
texts.marginal: SP flew an acceptable holding pattern, but drift correction was refined over successive circuits instead of being assessed at entry. The legs stayed within standards although the inbound intercepts were not consistent. SP is expected to evaluate drift on the first inbound leg and apply it immediately.

texts_at.0: With the IP determining the holding entry and calling the drift correction to apply outbound, SP followed the pattern on the controls while beginning to time the legs. Determining the entry and assessing drift on the first inbound leg without prompting have not yet been asked of SP. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin naming the entry type before determining it independently.
texts_at.1: SP flew the holding entry and pattern inside the standard required at this stage, the entry only marginally matching the published pattern before drift correction and leg timing were applied. The trend traces to the entry decision being made close to the fix rather than a little before it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to make the entry decision a little before the fix so the pattern matches published guidance from the first circuit.
texts_at.2: SP flew the holding entry and pattern inside the standard required at this stage, arriving at the inbound turn displaced from the pattern before the drift correction was adjusted. The trend traces to the outbound drift correction being under-applied on the first circuit. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply the full outbound drift correction from the first circuit so the displacement narrows further.
texts_at.3: SP determined the correct entry, flew the published pattern and applied drift correction so the inbound legs rolled out close to course, the small margin tracing to the correction being refined a circuit later than the first inbound leg allowed. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to assess drift on the first inbound leg so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP flew the holding entry and pattern with the inbound legs rolled out close to course, the drift correction adjusted after a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified the error from the course indication and the leg timing, adjusted the outbound correction and stabilized the next circuit without IP input, after arriving displaced from the pattern at the inbound turn. Assessing drift on the first inbound leg, rather than after arriving displaced, would remove even that adjustment. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent holding pattern technique.
texts_above.3: SP determined the correct entry, flew the published pattern and applied drift correction so that the inbound legs rolled out on course, timing started and adjusted at the correct points, circuits flown consistently. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined holding pattern technique.
texts_above.4: SP flew the entry and the holding pattern with the inbound course captured precisely and leg timing corrected to the target value from the first circuit, drift assessed early and applied accurately on the outbound leg. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to faultless holding pattern technique.

error_modes.label: Decision point discipline and missed approach execution

texts.0: SP, due to continuation bias after the profile had already degraded, pressed on past the point at which the missed approach was required. The published missed approach actions were not initiated and the aircraft remained in an unsuitable state. IP directed and then flew the go-around.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to abandon a procedure already begun, delayed the missed approach decision beyond the briefed point. The action was initiated only after the IP called for it, and the climb and configuration sequence lagged behind. The procedure was completed, but the decision was not the SP's own.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow assessment against the briefed decision criteria, hesitated briefly at the decision point. SP then made the decision independently, initiated the missed approach and flew the published climb and course. The hesitation did not affect the outcome and no IP input was needed.
texts.3: SP applied the briefed decision criteria at the correct point and executed the missed approach promptly. Power, attitude and configuration were sequenced correctly and the published track was flown. The decision was made without hesitation.
texts.4: SP evaluated the decision criteria ahead of the point and executed the missed approach immediately and cleanly. The climb, configuration change and navigation transition were flown as one continuous, unhurried sequence. The published track and altitude were captured precisely.
texts.marginal: SP made the correct decision inside the required window, but only after visibly weighing the option to continue. Execution after the decision met standards. SP is expected to commit to the briefed decision criteria the moment they are met.

texts_at.0: With the IP assessing the profile against the decision criteria and calling the missed approach when it was required, SP followed the go-around procedure on the controls after the call. Applying the briefed decision criteria and committing to the missed approach without prompting have not yet been asked of SP at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin stating the assessment against the criteria out loud before making the decision unaided.
texts_at.1: SP applied decision point discipline inside the standard required at this stage, initiating the missed approach only after a noticeable hesitation at the briefed point. The trend traces to the decision criteria being weighed again at the point itself rather than confirmed in advance. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the decision criteria before the point is reached so the action follows without hesitation.
texts_at.2: SP applied decision point discipline inside the standard required at this stage, hesitating briefly at the decision point before making the call independently. The trend traces to the assessment against the briefed criteria being slower than the point allowed for. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the assessment against the criteria before reaching the point so the hesitation is removed.
texts_at.3: SP applied the briefed decision criteria at the correct point and executed the missed approach promptly, the small margin tracing to the climb sequence being confirmed a moment after the decision rather than as part of it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to fold the climb sequence into the decision itself so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP applied the briefed decision criteria and executed the missed approach with the correct climb, configuration and track, the call to commit following a verbal prompt from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP made the decision independently, initiated the missed approach and flew the published climb and course without IP input, after a brief hesitation at the decision point. Confirming the decision criteria before the point is reached, rather than weighing them again at it, would remove even that hesitation. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good missed approach decision discipline.
texts_above.3: SP applied the briefed decision criteria at the correct point and executed the missed approach promptly, power, attitude and configuration sequenced correctly and the published track flown, the decision made without hesitation. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to very good missed approach decision discipline.
texts_above.4: SP evaluated the decision criteria ahead of the point and executed the missed approach immediately and cleanly, climb, configuration change and navigation transition flown as one continuous, unhurried sequence. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to excellent missed approach decision discipline.

error_modes.label: Transition from outside references to instrument flight

texts.0: SP, due to spatial disorientation on transitioning from outside references to the instruments, made control inputs against the indications rather than with them. Attitude, altitude and heading diverged at the same time and the SP did not accept the instrument picture. IP took control and re-established stable instrument flight.
texts.1: SP, due to conflicting vestibular cues after the transition to instruments, resisted the attitude indicator and held a sustained bank input. The SP returned to the instrument reference only after the IP verbally directed it. Control was recovered without intervention on the controls, but the transition was not managed independently.
texts.2: SP, due to a brief false sensation of bank on entering the instrument segment, allowed the attitude to deviate inside the tolerance band. SP recognized the conflict, deliberately transferred control to the attitude indicator and re-established the flight path. The recovery was made in good time and unaided.
texts.3: SP transitioned to instrument references cleanly and continued to fly attitude, altitude and heading from the instruments. Any sensory conflict was disregarded in favor of the indications. Aircraft control remained stable through each transition.
texts.4: SP moved between outside and instrument references with no disturbance at all to aircraft control. The instrument picture was accepted immediately and flown with confidence throughout the procedure. No sensory conflict was allowed to reach the control inputs.
texts.marginal: SP transitioned to instrument flight within standards, but the first seconds after each transition showed small control inputs that did not follow the indications. The resulting deviations stayed inside tolerance. SP is expected to establish the instrument scan before the transition so that control is continuous.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling attention to the attitude indicator at each transition and taking the correction if a sensory conflict was followed, SP followed on the controls through the transition while beginning to accept the instrument picture. Disregarding a sensory conflict without prompting has not yet been asked of SP at this stage. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin naming a sensory conflict out loud before disregarding it unaided.
texts_at.1: SP transitioned to instrument references inside the standard required at this stage, resisting the attitude indicator briefly before returning to it. The trend traces to a conflicting vestibular cue being followed for a moment rather than disregarded immediately on entry. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to disregard the conflicting cue from the first indication so the transition is continuous.
texts_at.2: SP transitioned to instrument references inside the standard required at this stage, attitude deviating briefly inside the tolerance band on entry to the segment. The trend traces to a false sensation of bank being followed for an instant before the indicator was trusted. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to transfer to the attitude indicator at the first sign of a sensory conflict so the deviation narrows further.
texts_at.3: SP transitioned to instrument references cleanly and continued to fly attitude, altitude and heading from the instruments, the small margin tracing to the transition itself taking a moment longer on the segment flown into the greatest sensory conflict. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to rehearse that specific transition so it matches the speed of the others.

texts_above.1: SP transitioned to instrument references and continued to fly attitude, altitude and heading from the instruments, disregarding a sensory conflict after a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the conflict, deliberately transferred control to the attitude indicator and re-established the flight path in good time and unaided, after a brief false sensation of bank on entering the instrument segment. Transferring to the attitude indicator at the first sign of the conflict, rather than after following it briefly, would remove even that deviation. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound instrument transition technique.
texts_above.3: SP transitioned to instrument references cleanly and continued to fly attitude, altitude and heading from the instruments, any sensory conflict disregarded in favor of the indications, aircraft control remaining stable through each transition. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed instrument transition technique.
texts_above.4: SP moved between outside and instrument references with no disturbance at all to aircraft control, the instrument picture accepted immediately and flown with confidence throughout the procedure. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exceptional instrument transition technique.
